issues.explanation: For stalking trauma, 'Betrayal' can be plausible if the stalker was known to the patient, but the profile provides no supporting items suggesting an interpersonal betrayal context. More importantly, 'Contamination' is typically associated with sexual assault or physical violation and is hard to reconcile clinically with stalking in the absence of any other items indicating assault, bodily intrusion, or abuse.

Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Contamination' point to different trauma meanings: interpersonal trust violation versus bodily violation. They can coexist in some cases, but with stalking alone and no corroborating memory, trigger, or threat items, this combination is clinically difficult to justify.

For stalking trauma, 'I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened' is hard to reconcile unless there was an additional sexual or physical assault element. On its face, this appraisal is clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

'Avoid Medical Care' implies avoidance centered on trauma-related examination, disclosure, or bodily injury/assault concerns, but there are no Memory, Threat, or Trigger items indicating injury, assault, or medical trauma. It is poorly matched to the rest of this stalking profile.

vignette:
Mele was 20, a first-year auditor living alone and trying to establish herself in a demanding office where long hours and careful attention were prized. The trauma began not as a single dramatic assault but as a pattern that gradually closed around her. A man she had briefly spoken to several times near her apartment and once outside the downtown building where she worked began appearing in places that should have been unrelated: across the street from her bus stop in the morning, near the coffee shop beneath her office, outside the grocery store she used after work. At first she told herself she might be imagining it, but the repetition stripped that explanation away. He would stand still and watch her. Once, as she left work after staying late to finish audit documentation, she saw him half-hidden by a parked car and felt the instant, sick certainty that he knew her routines better than she did. After that, ordinary parts of the city-an elevator opening into the lobby, footsteps behind her on the sidewalk, someone lingering too long near the entrance of her building-no longer felt neutral. They felt like proof that nowhere was protected.

In the weeks that followed, Mele came to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that safety depended on never relaxing. What frightened her most was not only that he had followed her, but what it seemed to reveal: that anyone could watch, wait, and intrude without warning. She became convinced she had to be on guard all the time. Walking to work, she scanned reflections in windows and checked who was behind her. At the office, where part of her job involved moving between conference rooms and records areas, she kept track of exits and noticed every unfamiliar face in the reception area. Even when she was seated at her desk reviewing spreadsheets, some part of her attention stayed fixed on whether someone might be outside the glass doors. Alongside that vigilance, her view of her future darkened. She had started adulthood expecting independence and possibility; now she said it felt as if her life had been destroyed by what happened, as though the ordinary confidence of being young and building a career had been taken from her and not returned.

Those beliefs began to shape how she lived. Because she was certain danger was everywhere and that any lapse could invite more harm, she started avoiding going out except when it seemed absolutely necessary. She took the most direct route between work and home and cut out errands that were not essential. If coworkers invited her to get dinner after a late close or celebrate the end of a busy week, she declined, telling herself that being out longer only increased the chances of being seen, followed, or trapped. The same conviction drained the meaning from anything that might have brought relief. Situations that could make her feel happy or hopeful began to feel almost intolerable, not because she had lost the capacity for pleasure entirely, but because allowing herself to enjoy them seemed unsafe and naive. If she accepted a social invitation or let herself look forward to a weekend plan, she felt she was forgetting the reality she now believed governed the world. In that sense, avoiding positive moments became part of staying alert.

Over time, her appraisals turned inward as well. Mele had come to believe that what had happened had ruined her life, and from there it was a short step to feeling that she herself should suffer for it. She would tell herself she deserved to suffer because of what happened, as though any comfort or ease would be undeserved. When she spent another evening alone in her apartment after work, eating something quick and ignoring messages from friends, there was a harsh logic to it in her mind: if the world was dangerous and her life already wrecked, then denying herself anything enjoyable felt fitting, almost morally required. The more she thought this way, the smaller her life became. Her work remained intact on paper, but colleagues had noticed she never joined group lunches and always left with visible tension, checking the street before stepping outside. She was still performing, but at the cost of constant strain and increasing isolation.

By the time she sought help, Mele was exhausted by the effort of maintaining this guarded life. What finally pushed her into treatment was not a new stalking incident but the recognition that she was structuring every day around threat and deprivation. She could see how little remained beyond work and vigilance. She was most afraid that this was permanent-that she would always live as if watched, always deny herself ordinary happiness, and never again feel that the world contained any safe place for her. At the same time, a small part of her hoped that if someone understood how completely this fear had reorganized her life, she might not have to keep punishing herself just to feel prepared.
